q: Can the original 1995 Fleischmann assembly be re-executed byte-for-byte from any surviving artifact (Sanger trace archive, TIGR Assembler source, or the ~19,687 sequencing reads at ~6× coverage), and if not, at what point in the pipeline chain does that reproducibility permanently fail — assembler code, primary reads, or gap-closure notebooks?
basis: The paper's headline *methodological* claim — that whole-genome random shotgun sequencing plus TIGR Assembler is sufficient to produce a complete circular bacterial chromosome — is the most historically consequential result in the article, but our replication explicitly could NOT test it. The 1995 raw Sanger traces are not deposited in any standard SRA-reusable form (BioProject PRJNA224116 hosts the assembly, not the reads); TIGR Assembler source has been superseded; the ~140 primer-walk gap-closure reactions are documented only in the paper's text. This is the single largest untested piece of the Fleischmann corpus and a real gap in genomics-history reproducibility, not a superficial 'find the code' problem.
next_steps: (1) FOIA / archival request to J. Craig Venter Institute (JCVI, successor to TIGR) for the 1995 Sanger trace archive on physical media — DAT tapes, DDS-3, or CD-R backups likely still exist in institutional storage. (2) Cross-reference with the NCBI Trace Archive (retired 2016) mirror at EBI/ENA (`https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/text-search?query=Fleischmann%201995%20Haemophilus`) — TIGR did submit some contemporaneous projects. (3) If reads recoverable, re-run modern assemblers (SPAdes, Flye, Unicycler) at matched ~6× coverage on the recovered reads to compare N50, gap count, and misassembly rate against the 1995 TIGR Assembler output. (4) If reads unrecoverable, subsample modern Illumina H. influenzae Rd KW20 short-read data (e.g. SRR* from strain KW20 resequencing) to ~6× and demonstrate whether *any* 1995-era-comparable input produces a closed circular assembly with 1990s-era algorithmic constraints. (5) Write up as a 'reproducibility of the first genome' historical-methods paper — this has never been done end-to-end.

q: The paper reports 1,743 predicted CDSs (1995), and RefSeq NC_000907.1 (2020 re-annotation) reports 1,721 CDSs of which 117 are pseudogenes. What is the *biological* status of the 22-gene delta and, more importantly, of the 117 pseudogenes — are these genuine loss-of-function events fixed in the KW20 laboratory strain, sequencing errors preserved as pseudogenes in RefSeq, or artifacts of a stricter modern CDS-calling threshold? Quantifying this matters because *H. influenzae* Rd is a workhorse strain for functional genomics and its 'pseudogene' set is treated as ground truth by dozens of downstream studies.
basis: Our replication reproduced the CDS count within re-annotation drift (−1.3%) but did NOT investigate what the 117 pseudogenes actually are. The paper predates the pseudogene concept as a systematic RefSeq category. There is no published pseudogene-by-pseudogene audit of NC_000907.1 that separates the three failure modes above; this is a real hole in the annotation-quality literature for a genome that has been re-sequenced dozens of times.
next_steps: (1) Extract all 117 pseudo-annotated features from NC_000907.1 with their `note` qualifiers explaining why RefSeq marked them pseudo. (2) For each, cross-check against short-read resequencing of a fresh KW20 stock (e.g. NCBI SRA runs for BioSample SAMN02603729 or a recent PATRIC/BV-BRC upload) at ≥50× coverage to determine whether the pseudogenizing lesion (frameshift, premature stop, in-frame deletion) is present in the strain, absent in the strain (⇒ likely 1995 sequencing error), or present but at reduced frequency (⇒ mixed culture). (3) For confirmed real pseudogenes, tabulate the functional-category distribution (are they enriched in restriction-modification, phage remnants, or metabolic redundancy?) — this speaks to Rd being a laboratory-adapted derivative of a wild isolate. (4) Publish the audited pseudogene list as a BV-BRC data-augmentation contribution.

q: The paper's Table on structural RNAs reports 54 tRNAs; NC_000907.1 has 57. Our replication counted +3 tRNAs (+5.6%) and flagged it as 'within re-annotation drift.' But *which specific three tRNA loci* were added between the 1995 annotation and modern RefSeq, and are they (a) genuine tRNAs missed by 1995-vintage tRNAscan-SE (before v1.4), (b) selenocysteine/pyrrolysine-related additions, (c) tRNA-like structures wrongly promoted to real tRNAs by modern tools, or (d) duplicated-isoacceptor tRNAs identified by whole-genome comparative analysis? This is a general problem across all pre-2000 bacterial genome papers with tRNA counts.
basis: Our replication tested the total tRNA count but did no per-locus comparison against the 1995 tRNA table. The delta is small but is exactly the kind of finding that gets copy-pasted into review articles as 'H. influenzae has 57 tRNAs' without provenance. tRNA-genes-per-genome is a functional-inference metric (codon-usage constraints, translation efficiency) and a wrong-by-3 count matters more than the percentage suggests for downstream metabolic-modeling.
next_steps: (1) Extract all 57 tRNA locus tags + coordinates + anticodon + amino-acid from NC_000907.1. (2) Re-annotate the 1995-vintage L42023 sequence with tRNAscan-SE v2.0 in default mode to obtain the modern call set. (3) Diff against the 1995 tRNA table (obtain via PDF once accessible; failing that, mine tRNAdb 2009 which cataloged historical H. influenzae tRNAs). (4) For each of the 3 delta loci, classify by mechanism (a-d above). (5) Publish as a supplementary correction / re-annotation note that BV-BRC / RefSeq can attach as a curator comment.

q: The paper claims 'densely coding' but does not tabulate a precise coding-density number; our replication measured 82.53% by interval-union of non-pseudo CDS parts. Yet this number is *not* directly comparable to what the paper meant, because in 1995 pseudogenes were not carved out. Recomputing INCLUSIVE of pseudo-CDSs gives a different number, and INCLUDING intergenic regulatory / ncRNA features moves it again. Genomes-are-densely-coding is a foundational bacterial-genomics claim that continues to be cited quantitatively, but with no standardized measure. What is the correct, community-adoptable definition of 'coding density' for a bacterial genome, and how does *H. influenzae* Rd rank once that definition is applied consistently across the ~500,000 bacterial genomes in NCBI/BV-BRC?
basis: Our replication surfaced this ambiguity concretely: we reported 82.53% under one reasonable definition (interval-union of non-pseudo CDS) but the paper's implicit definition (all predicted ORFs, no pseudogene carve-out, 1995 GeneMark) would yield a higher number. There is no ISO / IUBMB definition of 'coding density.' Comparative genomics papers routinely quote coding density as a bacterial-lifestyle proxy (obligate intracellular = higher density) but the numbers are not commensurate across studies.
next_steps: (1) Enumerate all definitional choices: (i) include/exclude pseudogenes; (ii) include/exclude non-coding RNA features (tRNA/rRNA/tmRNA/ncRNA/regulatory); (iii) interval-union vs sum-of-lengths (matters for overlapping ORFs); (iv) strand-aware vs strand-agnostic. (2) Compute all 16 combinations on a curated set of 20 well-annotated bacterial reference genomes (H. influenzae Rd + 19 others spanning lifestyle: E. coli MG1655, M. tuberculosis, M. genitalium, B. aphidicola, R. prowazekii, Synechocystis, etc.). (3) Show which definitional choices maximally scramble the ranking. (4) Propose a canonical definition + release a `bactcodedensity` PyPI package that returns all four principal variants with provenance. (5) Retroactively benchmark against ~100 highly-cited coding-density claims from the bacterial-genomics literature 1995–present to see how much they would change under the canonical definition.

q: The paper reports two Mu-like cryptic prophages and multiple simple-sequence repeats implicated in phase variation. Our replication observed only 3 `misc_feature` + 1 `repeat_region` annotations in NC_000907.1 — a striking under-annotation compared to the paper's detailed discussion. Where did the prophage and phase-variation-repeat annotations *go* between 1995 and 2020, and does the current NC_000907.1 record actually retain the biological information the original paper contributed, or has RefSeq's minimalist re-curation silently lost domain-expert annotation that no downstream user could recover without going back to the original PDF?
basis: Our replication surfaced a genuine annotation-provenance failure: the paper's substantive biological content about mobile elements and contingency loci is largely absent from the modern reference record for the strain the paper defined. This is a *systemic* problem — RefSeq re-annotation pipelines strip narrative annotation in favor of algorithmic feature-calling — and it means the field's 'reference' for H. influenzae Rd is now measurably less biologically informative than the 1995 paper.
next_steps: (1) Recover the paper's specific coordinates for the two Mu-like prophages and the phase-variation SSR loci (from Table 3 / Figure 4 / supplementary text). (2) Independently re-detect prophages on NC_000907.1 using PHASTER, VirSorter2, and CheckV; independently re-detect SSRs using imperfect-repeat finders (Tantan, IMPERFECT). (3) Cross-tabulate: what did the paper find, what do modern tools re-find on the same coordinates, what disappeared and why. (4) Reconstruct a 'lossless' *H. influenzae* Rd annotation that merges 1995 narrative annotation with modern algorithmic calls, submit as a GFF3 supplement to BV-BRC. (5) Generalize the audit to a random sample of pre-2000 bacterial genome papers to quantify the systemic 'RefSeq amnesia' problem and propose a remediation workflow.
